source.title: The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety
source.authors: Anton Korznikov; Andrey V. Galichin; Alexey Dontsov; Oleg Y. Rogov; I. Oseledets; Elena Tutubalina

record.file_problem: The text is a full paper. It contains an internal inconsistency: the main text reports 353 SAE features jailbreak at least five prompts, while Fig. 5's caption reports 668/1000.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses the previously reported refusal direction as a comparator for cosine similarity, but does not remove, add, or otherwise test the difference-in-means refusal direction or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports outcomes for random and SAE activation steering, not for the difference-in-means direction in the claim. It explicitly compares harmful SAE features with a previously reported refusal direction. Coefficients and layer selections used to choose settings are not separate outcome rows. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study steers with random and SAE vectors and reports its own attack's compliance rates. It never derives, ablates or adds the difference-in-means refusal direction, so it tests no version. Its only contact with the claim is Appendix E. There, cosine similarity between the top 30 jailbreaking SAE features and the Arditi et al. refusal direction is near zero (0.027 ± 0.0208). The authors read this, plus the layer profile, as evidence that steering does not simply suppress the refusal direction, which bears on V3. But cosine similarity between an added vector and the direction cannot show whether activations along the direction are suppressed after downstream nonlinear processing. No projection onto the direction and no refusal-rate test along it is reported. So this is discussion, not a test of V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that random and benign SAE steering systematically breaks safety, and that averaging 20 single-prompt random jailbreak vectors gives a universal attack. They also say jailbreaks do not simply suppress a refusal direction, but this rests only on near-zero cosine similarities of the steering vectors and on the layer profile, not on any measurement of the direction's activation. The universal attack is model-dependent: it fails for Qwen2.5-32B.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random unit vectors and SAE feature directions added at a fixed layer; does not derive a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction or ablate that direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported steering outcome varies with model, layer, coefficient, and prompt/category. The paper reports maximal vulnerability in middle or early layers and lower effectiveness in later layers; coefficient effects can be non-monotonic.

fits_no_version.finding: Random unit-vector steering at middle layers raises harmful compliance from 0% to roughly 1–18% depending on model, layer and coefficient; SAE features do slightly more.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Arbitrary or benign activation steering can break refusal on harmful requests without targeting a refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Many SAE features jailbreak some prompts but generalize poorly; the count reaching at least five prompts is reported inconsistently (353 vs 668).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering-induced jailbreak vulnerability is widespread but prompt-specific.

fits_no_version.finding: A benign 'brand identity' SAE feature applied via the Goodfire API produced harmful compliance on example prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign-concept SAE steering through public APIs can produce harmful outputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaging 20 single-prompt jailbreaking random vectors raises compliance on unseen prompts about 4× on average; this fails for Qwen2.5-32B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregated random jailbreak vectors form model-dependent universal steering attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: The top jailbreaking SAE feature directions are nearly orthogonal to the known refusal direction (mean cosine 0.027).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective jailbreak steering vectors need not be geometrically aligned with the refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: At coefficient 0.75, Llama3.1-8B loses less than 1% MMLU under random steering.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Moderate random steering can raise harmful compliance at small capability cost.

record.problems: The paper reports a conflicting count for SAE features that jailbreak at least five prompts (353 in the text versus 668/1000 in the Fig. 5 caption). The principal safety metric relies on an LLM judge; human validation reports 94% precision for harmful classifications from a sample of 100 selected responses, without a reported uncertainty interval. Several figure-based findings are described without exact numeric values. The cosine comparison does not establish a causal role for the refusal direction.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed figure-only values for layer and coefficient sweeps, category heatmaps, cross-category generalization, and per-model plots were not extracted where the text supplied no specific numeric outcome. These are shown in Figs. 2–5, 7, and 10. Selection criteria and coefficients used to tune settings were not treated as outcome rows.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction extracted, ablated or added; no refusal or capability measured under it.
No measurement of the refusal direction's activation under steering attacks; no training against its ablation.
No multi-direction, cone or affine analysis.
No separation of harmfulness from refusal.
No transfer across languages, variants or base/instruct.

missing.what: Per-feature cosine similarities with the refusal direction for the top jailbreaking features (e.g. feature 772, 35 prompts, cosine 0.0052). These could enrich R20 but bear on no version as a test.

record.verdict_notes: The Section 4.1 statement that steering 'doesn't simply suppress a pre-existing refusal direction' is an interpretive argument, not a measured result. A vector orthogonal to the refusal direction can still reduce its downstream projection. Appendix E misdescribes the Arditi direction as bypassing safety when added. The study never says which layer or extraction the direction came from. No verdicts are given because no row measures a version's effect.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is found or ablated; no addition of that direction is tested; harmless-request refusal and retained general capability under that direction are not tested.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The study tests steering attacks but does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of refusal is tested.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision is tested.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer of the claimed direction is tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or stages is conducted.
No reasoning-model test of the claimed direction is conducted.

rows.subject: Llama3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Computed cosine similarity between the 30 most harmful SAE features and a previously reported refusal direction.
rows.measure: Mean cosine similarity with refusal direction
rows.note: The authors characterize this as near-zero and say it argues against simple linear alignment as the primary mechanism for their SAE steering results.
rows.check: Measures cosine similarity between injected SAE decoder vectors and the refusal direction, not suppression of the direction's activation during the attack. It cannot show whether attacks work by suppressing the direction. The layer and extraction details of the refusal direction used are not stated. The paper also describes the direction as one that 'bypass[es] safety when added', the reverse of the original finding.

rows.note: This capability result is for random steering, not ablation or addition of the claimed refusal direction.
